episode_thesis: Rob Carver argues that bad years are a normal, mathematically expected part of trend following, that how a system sizes and exits positions (continuous volatility-scaled sizing versus stops) matters as much as signal speed in a V-shaped shock like April 2025, and that the right response to a drawdown is process discipline (check costs, compare to expected drawdown, keep diversification) rather than redesign. He also holds a bearish discretionary view on the US economy after tariffs and argues leveraged ETFs are toxic. Niels frames April 2025 as a stress test in which Treasuries and the dollar failed as safe havens, trend followers were wrong-footed in equities and FX but helped by commodities, and risk-management systems mostly worked as designed.

speakers.name: Rob Carver
speakers.role: Co-host; independent systematic futures trader, author on systematic trading; ex-AHL, trades his own money
speakers.speaker_note: Transcript spells him 'Rob Carver'. Corrections applied from the ledger: MT196-C09-2 is the 2024-25 tax year (about -15%, roughly a one-in-10-year event), with his previous worst year being April 2014 to April 2015; MT196-C18-3 is Niels describing the leveraged Nasdaq tweet, with Rob only saying it is not remotely a good idea. The 'Sebastian Valerie' paper is 'Breaking the Trend: How to Avoid Cherrypicked Signals'.

worldview_premises.premise: Bad years happen to well-diversified trend portfolios because everything goes wrong at once in a trendless year, not because of concentration in one market; a 2024-25 loss of about -15% was roughly a one-in-10-year event for him.
worldview_premises.support: His own P&L by asset class for the year: losses in equities, energies, FX, metals and bonds, with gains only in the S&P; natural gas worst. Worst previous year April 2014 to April 2015.

worldview_premises.premise: The longer a strategy runs, the larger its expected worst drawdown, so veteran funds hitting new worst drawdowns is mathematically unsurprising.
worldview_premises.support: Drawdowns grow over time in expectation (he is unsure if the growth follows the square root of time).

worldview_premises.premise: Because trend signals have a modest Sharpe ratio, it takes a very long time to tell statistically that a system has stopped working, so continuing is a matter of faith; systematic traders should in theory do nothing when the strategy underperforms, though in practice that is hard.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from Sharpe-ratio statistics; no calculation shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Variable position sizing (daily risk adjustment) makes the return distribution closer to normal with fewer outliers, while stop-based systems create larger outliers both ways; stops can close at the wrong moment, and outsized positions in a market that has run up (cocoa) are a source of downside outliers.
worldview_premises.support: Described by himself as a handwaving academic argument.

worldview_premises.premise: Capturing a V-shaped reversal such as April 2025 needs extremely fast trading; slightly too slow trading is whipsawed, a very wide stop simply holds, and a tight stop is triggered near the low.
worldview_premises.support: Walk-through of the S&P path around April 8-9, 2025.

worldview_premises.premise: Few quantitative variables predict when trend following will do well or badly, so meta-timing is not productive; the best answer to a client's worry is visibility into historical analogues.
worldview_premises.support: His own attempts at quantitative conditioning.

worldview_premises.premise: Costs are predictable while P&L is nearly random, so an annual cost check (commissions plus slippage versus mid) is the most reliable review; his costs were about 100 bp, in line with the backtest, and passive limit orders beat the conservative half-spread assumption.
worldview_premises.support: His own annual review.

worldview_premises.premise: Different trend indicators are highly correlated, so no single one is uniquely best, but once automated, extra signals cost nothing; a single calibrated EMA (112 days) can represent the trend universe.
worldview_premises.support: Comparison of his own five or six indicators across speeds; the Breaking the Trend paper's mathematical link between exponential and simple moving averages.

worldview_premises.premise: Relative (cross-sectional) signals and style diversification held up in the 2024-25 trendless regime: of about 50 forecasting variables, only fast relative momentum, relative carry and relative value skew made money.
worldview_premises.support: His own attribution by indicator; even carry (especially slowest) lost.

worldview_premises.premise: US Treasuries may no longer be the default safe haven: US policy seems designed to create stagflation so the normal central bank reaction (cutting rates) may not apply, and traditional buyers (China) may avoid Treasuries in a crisis born in the US; breakdown of institutional rules is bad for US assets.
worldview_premises.support: Two competing explanations he calls policy-reaction and flows; the FT 'Giffen good' article framing.

worldview_premises.premise: Tariffs lag in the data: Q1 GDP was not affected by them, CEOs avoid honest forward earnings guidance, and the real-economy effect and earnings downgrades come later, producing a deep technical recession.
worldview_premises.support: FT articles (Martin Wolf's Road Runner analogy), Bezos tariff example, noted distortion of Q1 GDP by gold flows and import front-running.

worldview_premises.premise: Funds that can make 100% in good years can lose 30-60% in bad years; whether that is Kelly-optimal matters less than whether investors can stomach it, and fixed 2-4x leverage on already risky assets is far beyond Kelly sizing.
worldview_premises.support: Brief reasoning on Kelly; leveraged ETF example.

worldview_premises.premise: Leveraged ETFs reset daily so compounding makes adverse, choppy moves devastating (a 4x S&P ETF down 52% year to date versus S&P about -4.5%) and carry high expense ratios (about 295 bp).
worldview_premises.support: His own data download for his new book; quoted year-to-date figures.

worldview_premises.premise: Practical market-structure knowledge (contract quotation, settlement, data cleaning) is essential in systematic futures work.
worldview_premises.support: Career experience; advice to a young quant.

worldview_premises.premise: In extreme stress liquidity can vanish: in the first days after Liberation Day some positions had no bid and could not be sold.
worldview_premises.support: His own attempt to sell positions.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers form a family tree with distinct lineages (US pit-trading wing, British quantitative wing, Scandinavian), which explains differences of opinion about sizing and position changes.
worldview_premises.support: Substack article on industry history; his AHL background.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why April 2025 hurt different trend followers differently

steps.from: Liberation Day shock drives a sharp equity sell-off (S&P about 20% off its high)
steps.to: Trend followers cut or reverse equity and FX positions, some via stops
steps.why: Trend and risk rules react to drawdown and volatility

steps.from: Equity market V-reverses within days (bottom April 8-9)
steps.to: Tight-stop systems are flat with a loss booked; wide-stop systems hold; continuous sizing systems are down then sideways at one third of normal risk
steps.why: Position-capture method determines participation after the reversal

steps.from: Fastest models catch part of the initial bounce
steps.to: Later whipsaw erases it; moves too fast for even fast models (overnight gaps)

steps.from: Treasuries and the dollar sold off with equities
steps.to: Traditional hedge legs failed; gains came from commodities (energies, grains) and short rates
steps.why: Safe-haven status shifted when the crisis originated in the US

mechanism_chains.evidence: April 2025 index results: BTOP50 -3.49%, SG CTA -4.47%, SG Trend -4.98% (-9.41% YTD), short-term traders -0.86%, Bridge flat-fee trend -6.24%; Rob's own -5.5%; large trend followers -1% to -10%.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Depends on speed and the path; in a slower, trending sell-off, stops and sizing would behave differently. Rob notes he has not looked at individual market P&L.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why Treasuries failed as a safe haven in the tariff shock

steps.from: US policy seen as stagflationary (stagnation plus tariff inflation)
steps.to: Central bank reaction function (cut rates when growth weakens) may not apply
steps.why: Supply shock raises inflation while growth falls

steps.from: Crisis born in the US and breakdown of institutional rules
steps.why: Flows-based explanation: the US is hurt most

steps.to: Bonds hedge less; Swiss franc retains haven behaviour (Niels)
steps.why: Recency bias from a 40-year falling-rate cycle may be ending (Niels)

mechanism_chains.evidence: April 2025 price action; the Giffen-good analogy of the FT article.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Both explanations are stated as competing; neither is tested, and bonds partly recovered later in the month (Niels).

mechanism_chains.topic: From tariffs to a US recession (Rob's discretionary view)

steps.from: Tariffs hit goods in transit and stockpiles run down
steps.to: Real-economy data and earnings deteriorate with a lag
steps.why: Q1 GDP unaffected by tariffs; CEOs avoid honest forward guidance

steps.to: Technical recession deep enough that the equity market cannot stay where it is
steps.why: Expected earnings downgrades and demand destruction

steps.from: Cash earning about 4% against equity expected return of maybe 4% with large downside
steps.to: Stay in cash in the long-only portfolio

mechanism_chains.evidence: FT commentary (Wolf, Bezos), Q1 GDP quirks (gold, import spike).
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Rob admits the call looks wrong so far because the market rebounded, and that he would be long equities in his systematic portfolio if equities rise.

steps.from: Daily reset of 2-4x leverage on volatile assets
steps.to: Compounding losses in choppy markets (4x S&P ETF -52% versus S&P -4.5%)

steps.why: Product designed for short-term exposure management

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Short holding periods in trending markets (not discussed).

decision_process.practice: Adjust positions daily to risk (variable position sizing), which automatically cut risk to about a third of normal as the trend became unclear (less in equities).
decision_process.why: Avoids both the stop-out and the oversized exposure outliers.

decision_process.practice: Run about 50 forecasting variables (several trend indicators at multiple speeds, carry, relative momentum, value skew) and keep adding signals because additional automated signals cost nothing.
decision_process.why: Diversification across styles; relative signals held up in 2024-25.

decision_process.practice: Dynamically select positions from a larger instrument universe even though year-to-year return differences are noisy.
Keep about 50-60% in trend and add non-trend systems only when confident in them.
decision_process.why: More diversified than many peers; trend remains the core.

decision_process.practice: Annual review includes a cost check (commissions plus slippage versus mid price at order time), which should match the backtest (just under 100 bp).
decision_process.why: Costs are predictable, P&L is almost random.

decision_process.practice: Do not redesign after a bad year: the same review should be asked after an exceptional year and changes made only if evidence is clear. Compare the current drawdown with the probability of such a drawdown in a comparable period (about 30% over 12 years) and with backtest drawdowns.
Treat a 50% drawdown (far beyond the backtest and expectation) as a real concern; otherwise follow the process.
decision_process.why: Statistical bound from backtest and simulation.

decision_process.practice: Use passive limit orders first and switch to market orders if necessary; conservative backtest assumes paying half the spread.
decision_process.why: Lower realised slippage than the backtest assumption.

decision_process.practice: Raised the allocation to trend at the end of the previous tax year after trend's best quarter in 25 years, which meant the later losses hit a larger capital base.
decision_process.why: Not a deliberate timing call; the outcome illustrates the give-back risk of adding capital after a strong run.

decision_process.practice: In the discretionary long-only portfolio he sold all remaining US stocks around Liberation Day and went to cash, calling it his biggest discretionary decision ever.
decision_process.why: Bearish US economy view; cash at 4%.

speakers.evidence_style: Mostly own track record and own data (P&L by market and indicator, cost analysis), plus simple mathematics of drawdowns and Sharpe ratios; first-principles reasoning on position-sizing; sceptical of meta-timing. Discretionary macro views rely on FT commentary and reasoning about lags; he is open about his call looking wrong so far.

current_views.view: Bearish on the US economy: expects a deep technical recession and equity weakness; prefers cash (about 4%) in his long-only portfolio over equities.
current_views.reasoning: Tariffs lag; earnings downgrades to come; Q1 GDP distorted by gold and import front-running; institutional breakdown is bad for US assets.

current_views.view: US Treasuries may not be the go-to safe asset in this crisis; the normal central bank reaction function may not apply if policy produces stagflation.
current_views.reasoning: Stagflation policy mix and flows away from US assets.

current_views.view: His own April 2025 return was -5.5%, roughly in line with the industry, and the 2024-25 tax year about -15%, a one-in-10-year event; the strategy is not broken.
current_views.reasoning: Industry comparison: SG CTA about -10% versus his about -14.7% at higher volatility; probability of such a drawdown in 12 years about 30%.

current_views.view: Leveraged ETFs are toxic and the proliferation of 3-4x products is alarming.
current_views.reasoning: Daily reset compounding, cost, Kelly-exceeding leverage.

current_views.view: Pure trend is open to question after a long weak stretch (most firms diversified into other strategies), but he accepts that trend-is-dead worries have recurred and the industry survived.
current_views.reasoning: Winton and Aspect history from the Substack article read aloud.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host, Top Traders Unplugged; trend-following allocator and industry observer
speakers.speaker_note: Transcript spells him 'Neils Castro Larson'. He reports index numbers as of April 30/May 1, 2025, early manager indications, and describes the leveraged Nasdaq tweet (ledger correction for MT196-C18-3). 'Bill Dunn' comment is his: he says he worked for Bill Dunn.

worldview_premises.premise: Safe-haven assets are changing: bonds' safe-haven status may be recency bias from a 40-year falling-rate cycle; the Swiss franc still seems to retain safe-haven behaviour.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of April 2025; admits he may be talking his book (Swiss resident) but denies it.

worldview_premises.premise: In stress months commodities again delivered trend-following gains, while equities and currencies were headwinds in April 2025.
worldview_premises.support: Early manager indications; no precise attribution.

worldview_premises.premise: Dispersion between trend followers is usual and comes from speed, risk management and markets traded; hard-stop versus continuous-signal systems may differ materially in a V-shaped reversal.
worldview_premises.support: CFM research on dispersion; reasoning.

worldview_premises.premise: Funds with large open profits (high flyers) risk big give-backs, so investors entering after a hot streak face outsized drawdown risk.
worldview_premises.support: A fund he noted being hit hard in April 2025.

worldview_premises.premise: Risk management systems worked as designed in April 2025, so a down month for managers who followed process is normal and not evidence of strategy failure; investors should not redeem on a bad month (November 2021 example).
worldview_premises.support: Early data; November 2021 was a bad day followed by one of the best 12 months for many managers.

worldview_premises.premise: Portable alpha products (trend overlay on equity beta) looked bad in April 2025 with negative alpha and flat beta even though they did what they are designed to do.
worldview_premises.support: Imagined from index moves, not from reported results.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following had its best quarter in about 25 years in Q1 2024, then became much more challenging from April 2024.
worldview_premises.support: Index history.

worldview_premises.premise: The industry has survived the recurrent 'is trend following dead' question; Winton diversified away from trend, did poorly when CTAs did well, and has since rebuilt its trend allocation, while Aspect stuck to trend.
worldview_premises.support: Substack article read aloud; his industry knowledge.

worldview_premises.premise: There is a fine balance between simplicity and over-complication in trend systems and it makes a big difference.
worldview_premises.support: Past podcast discussions.

mechanism_chains.topic: Stop-out versus continuous participation in a V reversal

steps.from: A stop-based follower is stopped out in the sell-off
steps.to: Cannot re-enter until a new signal, missing the bounce
Different April P&L from stop systems
steps.why: Position adjusts with the signal rather than switching off

mechanism_chains.evidence: Observed performance differences among managers he can see online.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Rob adds that the real difference is the speed and capture method combined; a V reversal is extreme.

decision_process.practice: Track a trend barometer (52 at end of April 2025, a short-term measure) plus BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders and Bridge flat-fee trend indices against MSCI World, S&P 500 and bonds.
decision_process.why: Weekly health check of the category.

decision_process.practice: When evaluating managers, look at speed, risk management and markets traded as sources of dispersion, and consider open-profit levels of funds.
decision_process.why: Dispersion is usual; give-back risk for new entrants.

speakers.evidence_style: Index tables, early manager reports, news and anecdote; relies on guests for mechanics. Acknowledges the limit of early data.

current_views.view: April 2025 was a stress test: CTAs lost on the V-reversal in equities and FX, Treasuries and the dollar failed as hedges, commodities and short-term rates helped; the largest trend followers lost 1-10% in April and were between slightly up and -15-18% YTD.
current_views.reasoning: Early manager reports and index results.

current_views.view: Short-term models did better in the first half of April, but later reversals erased most of it; the fast models were still too slow for some moves.
Risk management systems held up and a down month is within normal range; no sign that trend following is broken.
Bonds may stop providing cover if rates trend higher after a 40-year falling-rate cycle.

disagreements.topic: Stops versus continuous signals as the explanation for April dispersion

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: April may differ materially between hard-stop systems and continuous-signal systems because a stopped-out system cannot re-enter before a new signal.

positions.speaker: Rob Carver
positions.position: Two separate drivers: signal speed and position-capture method; capturing the bounce needed extremely fast trading, wide stops simply held, and continuous sizing was down then flat.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Bond safe-haven status may be recency bias from a 40-year falling-rate cycle.

positions.speaker: Rob Carver
positions.position: Two competing explanations: stagflationary policy that breaks the central bank reaction function, and flows (traditional buyers such as China avoid Treasuries in a crisis born in the US).

disagreements.topic: Should a veteran trend system react to a long drawdown

positions.speaker: Rob Carver
positions.position: Do nothing in theory; only a drawdown well beyond backtest (for example 50%) is a real concern; avoid redesign and keep trend as 50-60% of the book while adding confident non-trend systems.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Surprised that managers with 30 years of experience hit their worst-ever drawdown, and notes investors will want to redeem; asks how to keep them from projecting.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Ledger correction: Rob's -15% is the April 2024 to April 2025 tax year, not his worst-ever year (April 2014 to April 2015); the later figure is -14.7%.
Ledger correction: Niels, not Rob, describes the leveraged Nasdaq tweet (7% a year becomes 21% with 3x); Rob's daily-reset explanation comes later.

Index figures are early and partial (as of April 30/May 1), the ledger line for April omits the SG CTA YTD (-6.88%) and BTOP50 YTD (-3.54%) given in the transcript, and the trend barometer of 52 is a short-term measure Niels does not define.
Rob has not looked at individual market P&L for April; his claim about the fastest models is an expectation of whipsaw afterwards, not a measured result.
The statement that worst drawdown grows with time is mathematical in expectation but Rob is unsure about the growth rate; the 30% probability over 12 years is quoted without the model.
Rob's bearish call (cash over equities) conflicted with the market rebound he admits; his systematic portfolio remains long if equities rise.
Niels says portable alpha did badly from imagination rather than reported results.
Rob says even the slowest carry signal lost money in 2024-25, contradicting the usual diversifier role of carry; he does not explain why.
Rob's costs claim (about 100 bp, in line with backtest) is one number without breakdown; passive-order slippage advantage is asserted.
Rob raised trend allocation at the end of the tax year before the drawdown, which conflicts with his own advice against adding after strong runs.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs these speakers treat as leading: tariff pass-through (goods in transit, stockpiles) to Q2-Q3 US GDP and earnings guidance; direction of Treasury yields and whether Treasuries rally on bad news (central bank reaction function); dollar and Swiss franc behaviour in stress; trend barometer; speed and position-capture method of trend models in V-shaped markets; commodity trends (energies, grains). Horizon: months for the tariff-recession call; the trend drawdown question is statistical and multi-year.
reader_inferences: (reader) Rob's account implies that variable position sizing behaves like an automatic reduction of exposure when signals become unclear, which gives a flat P&L after a shock instead of a clear stop-out; it protects against whipsaw but forfeits recoveries.

(reader) The 2024-25 pattern (only relative signals making money, every outright trend and even carry lost) suggests the loss was a trendless regime for outright trend rather than a failure of any one market, consistent with his diversified-portfolio argument.
(reader) Niels's and Rob's views on safe-haven change point to the same observable: whether Treasuries rally on bad US news. Neither provides a test beyond April 2025.
